description: A X-Earth é uma equipe formada por estudantes de Engenharia da Computação entusiastas de tecnologia, programação e eletrônica. Gostamos de colocar a mão na massa para resolver problemas reais, unindo desde a lógica de software até projetos envolvendo hardware e sistemas embarcados. Somos focados, colaborativos e temos facilidade para transformar ideias em protótipos funcionais em pouco tempo. Buscamos pessoas motivadas e com vontade de construir algo legal em conjunto.
summary:
During a mission to Mars, astronauts may need to make decisions about their health before they can contact a medical team on Earth. But a reading on a screen is not very useful if they cannot tell when it was taken or whether the information is reliable.

We developed PIP Health, a browser-based prototype that brings together six health indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, glucose, sleep, and mood. It includes interactive charts, a 3D body visualization, health check-ins, and a way to record follow-up actions.

Our solution focuses on making health data easier to understand. Each reading shows its source, timestamp, and availability, helping the crew distinguish recent measurements from outdated, missing, or invalid information. Records are stored locally, allowing the application to work offline after its initial setup. We also used NASA research and interface guidelines to support our design decisions.

This matters because future missions to Mars will require astronauts to become more independent. PIP Health explores how clear information can help crews monitor changes, recognize uncertainty, and decide when further evaluation is needed, even when communication with Earth is delayed.

All medical readings are simulated, and the prototype does not provide diagnoses.
details:
Imagine being halfway to Mars and noticing an unusual health reading. Before deciding what to do, you need to know whether the measurement is recent, where it came from, and whether the sensor was working properly. Without that context, even a well-designed dashboard can be misleading.

We built PIP Health to explore this problem. It is an interactive, browser-based health monitoring prototype designed around a fictional crew traveling to Mars.

The application brings together six health indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, glucose, sleep duration, and mood. Users can explore their readings through charts, an interactive 3D human model, and a dashboard that shows how measurements change over time.

A key part of our design is data reliability. Instead of simply displaying a number, PIP Health identifies its source, timestamp, and current data status. It distinguishes recent measurements from outdated, missing, unavailable, unknown, or invalid information. An old reading is never treated as proof that an astronaut is healthy.

Crew members can also complete simulated health check-ins, record sleep and mood, review historical measurements, and save follow-up actions locally.

Our goal is to make health information easier to interpret when astronauts cannot immediately contact medical specialists on Earth.

PIP Health is designed around three practical needs: understanding the available information, recognizing when something is uncertain, and keeping useful records during communication interruptions.

The prototype uses local browser storage and an offline-capable application shell. After the first online load, users can reopen the application and access locally stored demonstration records without an internet connection.

For future missions to Mars, where communication delays can make immediate assistance impossible, this approach could contribute to more independent health monitoring. The same principles could also be useful in remote environments on Earth where reliable internet access is limited.

We developed the application using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. Shared UI components help maintain a consistent interface, while Recharts supports historical data visualization and the interactive 3D model provides a visual way to explore the fictional crew's health information.

Zod is used for data validation, and Dexie with IndexedDB manages local browser storage. We also used automated tests and browser-based verification to examine application behavior, accessibility, and data handling.

The project draws on NASA's Human Research Program, NASA-STD-3001 guidance for crew interfaces, and historical research from the NASA Open Science Data Repository. These resources informed our design decisions and scientific context.

We chose not to build another dashboard that simply labels measurements as good or bad. Our main idea was to make uncertainty visible.

A measurement can be recent but still require interpretation. A missing value should remain missing, rather than becoming a misleading zero. A disconnected source should not appear to be providing live information.

We combined these principles with interactive visualization, fictional crew scenarios, clear status indicators, and local recordkeeping to create a demonstration that people can explore rather than just watch.

Throughout development, we considered accessibility, information clarity, data provenance, offline access, and the risks of presenting incomplete information as a medical conclusion.

All crew identities and health measurements in the demonstration are fictional or simulated. Historical NASA research is presented separately from current simulated readings. The 3D visualization is illustrative, not a medical scan.

PIP Health does not connect to real medical sensors, make diagnoses, prescribe treatment, or claim certification or endorsement by NASA. It is an educational prototype intended to demonstrate a practical approach to astronaut health information management.
